---
title: "Neighbourhood covariates"
subtitle: "An experiment: ten Census 2021 measures of diversity, migration, deprivation and work, added one at a time to Value Added v2.1. Do they explain the place effects, or something else?"
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
source(here::here("R", "site_helpers.R"))
N <- readRDS(here::here("data", "neighbourhood_covariates.rds"))
R <- N$res
r1 <- function(g, m, col) R[[col]][R$group == g & R$model == m]
cf <- function(g, m, term) { x <- R$coefs[[which(R$group == g & R$model == m)]]; 100 * (exp(x$est[x$term == term]) - 1) }
ctt <- function(g, m, term) { x <- R$coefs[[which(R$group == g & R$model == m)]]; x$est[x$term == term] / x$se[x$term == term] }
SO <- "School's own White British share"
p1 <- function(x) sprintf("%+.1f%%", x)
GCOL <- c("All pupils" = LPURPLE, "Disadvantaged pupils" = DPURPLE)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## An experiment, not a change to the model

Value Added v2.1 is unchanged. This page tests candidate terms, on the
same school-years and the same specification, to see what they would do.
Everything is published data: Census 2021 tables for Output Areas and
the January 2026 school census.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## In short

- **The largest gain is not a place measure.** It is the school's own share of White British pupils, which v2.1 does not have. For disadvantaged pupils, one standard deviation more goes with `r p1(r1("disadvantaged", SO, "pct"))` Attainment 8, all else equal. Once it is in, the neighbourhood's ethnic make-up adds little: what looked like a neighbourhood effect was mostly who the pupils are.
- **Neighbourhood deprivation, beyond qualifications, does matter.** At the same share of graduates, more multiply deprived households around a school go with *higher* results for disadvantaged pupils. This survives the school's own composition.
- **Together they take a fifth off the local authority effects for disadvantaged pupils, and over a third off the regional ones.** For all pupils, authority effects barely change.
- **About a third of Brighton and Hove's effect goes with these measures.** Its neighbourhoods are more deprived than their graduate share suggests.
:::

## The measures {#sec-measures}

Each is built exactly as neighbourhood education is: the average over the
`r N$k` Output Areas nearest each school, standardised across schools.

| Measure | Census 2021 table |
|---|---|
| White British (%); ethnic diversity (the chance two residents are from different groups, across 19) | TS021 |
| Born outside the UK (%) | TS004 |
| Cannot speak English well or at all (%) | TS029 |
| Arrived from abroad in the last year (%) | TS019 |
| Households deprived in two or more of four dimensions: employment, education, health, housing (%) | TS011 |
| Social renting (%) | TS054 |
| Routine, semi-routine or never worked (%); higher professional (%) | TS062 |
| Lone parents with dependent children (%) | TS003 |

Several move together closely. White British and born outside the UK
correlate at `r sprintf("%.2f", N$cors["z_wbri", "z_born_abroad"])`.
Higher professional correlates with neighbourhood education at
`r sprintf("%.2f", N$cors["z_l4", "z_higher_prof"])`, and routine work
with it at `r sprintf("%.2f", N$cors["z_l4", "z_routine"])`. So read the
measures in families, not one by one. To these is added the **school's own
share of White British pupils** (January 2026 census). It is a pupil
measure, not a neighbourhood one, and v2.1 has no pupil ethnicity, only
English as an additional language.

## One at a time {#sec-one}

```{r}
#| label: fig-one
#| fig-cap: "Each measure added on its own to the v2.1 model: the difference in Attainment 8 with one standard deviation more (%), with 95% intervals, for all pupils and disadvantaged pupils. Maximum likelihood, the same school-years throughout."
#| fig-height: 5.6
one <- R |> filter(n_terms == 1) |>
  mutate(grp = ifelse(group == "all", "All pupils", "Disadvantaged pupils"),
         lo = 100 * (exp(est - 1.96 * se) - 1), hi = 100 * (exp(est + 1.96 * se) - 1))
lev <- one |> filter(group == "disadvantaged") |> arrange(pct) |> pull(model)
ggplot(one |> mutate(model = factor(model, lev)), aes(pct, model, colour = grp)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = GCOL, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "% difference in Attainment 8 per standard deviation", y = NULL) + theme_note(11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

For all pupils every effect is small: about one per cent per standard
deviation at most. For disadvantaged pupils they are three to five times
larger. Disadvantaged pupils do better around schools in diverse,
migrant, less English-speaking and more deprived neighbourhoods, and
worse in White British and professional ones. The school's own White
British share is the strongest single term:
`r p1(r1("disadvantaged", SO, "pct"))` for disadvantaged pupils and
`r p1(r1("all", SO, "pct"))` for all.

## Composition or place? {#sec-composition}

A neighbourhood's ethnic make-up and a school's pupils go together. The
question is whether the neighbourhood matters *beyond* who the pupils
are. With the school's own White British share in the model:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-comp
#| tbl-cap: "The school's own White British share with neighbourhood measures alongside: each term's effect (% per SD, with its t value), for disadvantaged pupils and all pupils."
mods <- c("School's own + neighbourhood White British", "School's own + neighbourhood deprivation")
terms <- c(z_sch_wbri = "School's own White British share", z_wbri = "Neighbourhood White British",
           z_deprived2 = "Neighbourhood deprivation (2+ dimensions)")
bind_rows(lapply(mods, function(m) bind_rows(lapply(c("disadvantaged", "all"), function(g) {
  x <- R$coefs[[which(R$group == g & R$model == m)]]
  tibble(Model = m, Group = ifelse(g == "all", "All pupils", "Disadvantaged"), Term = terms[x$term],
         `% per SD` = sprintf("%+.1f", 100 * (exp(x$est) - 1)), t = sprintf("%.1f", x$est / x$se))
})))) |>
  kt(align = "lllrr") |> kableExtra::collapse_rows(columns = 1:2, valign = "top")
```

- **Ethnicity is mostly composition.** With the school's own share in, the neighbourhood's White British share shrinks from `r p1(r1("disadvantaged", "White British (%)", "pct"))` to `r p1(cf("disadvantaged", mods[1], "z_wbri"))` for disadvantaged pupils, and to nothing clear for all pupils (`r p1(cf("all", mods[1], "z_wbri"))`, t `r sprintf("%.1f", ctt("all", mods[1], "z_wbri"))`). The model fits barely better with both than with the school's own share alone (AIC `r sprintf("%.0f", r1("disadvantaged", mods[1], "aic_change"))` against `r sprintf("%.0f", r1("disadvantaged", SO, "aic_change"))`).
- **Deprivation is place.** Neighbourhood deprivation keeps its effect alongside the school's composition: `r p1(cf("disadvantaged", mods[2], "z_deprived2"))` per SD for disadvantaged pupils (t `r sprintf("%.1f", ctt("disadvantaged", mods[2], "z_deprived2"))`) and `r p1(cf("all", mods[2], "z_deprived2"))` for all. At the same share of graduates and the same pupils, a school in a more multiply deprived neighbourhood does a little better. One reading is that the qualification term overstates how advantaged some graduate-rich but deprived neighbourhoods are: places with many graduates alongside poor housing and health.

## Do they explain the place effects? {#sec-place}

```{r}
#| label: fig-place
#| fig-cap: "How much the local authority and region variances change when each set of terms is added (%). Negative: the terms account for part of what the authority or region effects were picking up."
#| fig-height: 4.8
SETS_SHOW <- c("Diversity and migration", "Deprivation and work", "All ten", SO,
               "School's own + neighbourhood deprivation", "School's own + all ten")
pl <- R |> filter(model %in% SETS_SHOW) |>
  select(group, model, `Local authority` = la_var_change, Region = reg_var_change) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(`Local authority`, Region), names_to = "level", values_to = "chg") |>
  mutate(grp = ifelse(group == "all", "All pupils", "Disadvantaged pupils"), model = factor(model, rev(SETS_SHOW)))
ggplot(pl, aes(chg, model, fill = grp)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ level) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GCOL, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(sprintf("%+.0f", x), "%")) +
  labs(x = "Change in variance (%)", y = NULL) + theme_note(11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

For **disadvantaged pupils**, the school's composition with neighbourhood
deprivation takes `r sprintf("%.0f", -r1("disadvantaged", "School's own + neighbourhood deprivation", "la_var_change"))`%
off the local authority variance and
`r sprintf("%.0f", -r1("disadvantaged", "School's own + neighbourhood deprivation", "reg_var_change"))`%
off the regional variance. Part of why disadvantaged pupils do better in
London and some cities than in the South East or coastal towns is who the
pupils are and what their neighbourhoods are like, at the same intake
otherwise.

For **all pupils**, authority effects barely change and regional ones
grow. The measures account for differences *within* regions, which leaves
the differences between them larger. For most pupils, what makes an
authority's schools do better is not in these measures.

## Brighton and Hove {#sec-bh}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bh
#| tbl-cap: "Brighton and Hove's local authority effect (% of Attainment 8) in the v2.1 model and with terms added."
bm <- c("Baseline (v2.1)", SO, "Households deprived in 2+ dimensions (%)", "School's own + neighbourhood deprivation",
        "School's own + deprivation and work", "School's own + all ten")
R |> filter(model %in% bm) |> select(group, model, bh) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = bh) |>
  mutate(m = factor(model, bm)) |> arrange(m) |>
  transmute(Model = model, `All pupils` = sprintf("%+.1f%%", all), Disadvantaged = sprintf("%+.1f%%", disadvantaged)) |>
  kt(align = "lrr")
```

Brighton and Hove's effect is one of the largest in England
([its own page](bh_effect.qmd)). Its schools' pupils are mostly White
British, so adding the school's composition, if anything, *raises* the
effect. Neighbourhood deprivation and work lower it, from
`r p1(r1("all", "Baseline (v2.1)", "bh"))` to
`r p1(r1("all", "School's own + deprivation and work", "bh"))` for all
pupils, and from `r p1(r1("disadvantaged", "Baseline (v2.1)", "bh"))` to
`r p1(r1("disadvantaged", "School's own + deprivation and work", "bh"))` for
disadvantaged pupils. The city's neighbourhoods have many graduates, but
also more households deprived on the Census measures than that suggests. Neighbourhood
education alone makes them look more advantaged than they are. About a
third of the effect goes with that; the rest is still unexplained.

## What it means for the model {#sec-means}

- **A candidate for v2.2: pupils' ethnicity.** DfE's contextual value
  added, in the performance tables until 2011, included pupils' ethnicity. Progress 8 does not,
  and nor does v2.1. The evidence here is that leaving it out matters most
  for disadvantaged pupils. Whether to put it in is a question of what the
  measure is for. Adjusting for it would stop schools with many White
  British disadvantaged pupils looking worse for it. It would also take a
  real difference in results out of view. It belongs with the review's
  other recommendations.
- **A candidate for neighbourhood: deprivation beside education.** Adding
  household deprivation to neighbourhood education makes the
  neighbourhood term fairer to graduate-rich but deprived places.
- **What is left of place.** Even with all of it, most of the local
  authority effects remain, especially for all pupils. What makes some
  authorities' schools do better than their intakes predict is not in the
  Census.

## How it was done {#sec-how}

Each model is the full v2.1 specification for its group, with the same
random effects for year and region/local authority, fitted by maximum
likelihood so that AIC can be compared. Every fit uses the same
`r format(r1("all", "Baseline (v2.1)", "rows"), big.mark = ",")` school-years for all pupils and
`r format(r1("disadvantaged", "Baseline (v2.1)", "rows"), big.mark = ",")` for disadvantaged pupils
(those with every measure). The school's own White British share is from
January 2026 and is used for every year, since earlier school census files
in the performance tables do not include ethnicity. Neighbourhoods are
the `r N$k` nearest Output Areas to the school, not pupils' homes.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-all
#| tbl-cap: "Every model: the change in AIC against v2.1 (negative is better), and in the local authority and region variances."
R |> filter(model != "Baseline (v2.1)") |>
  transmute(Group = ifelse(group == "all", "All pupils", "Disadvantaged"), Model = model,
            `% per SD` = ifelse(is.na(pct), "", sprintf("%+.2f", pct)), `AIC change` = sprintf("%.0f", aic_change),
            `Authority variance` = sprintf("%+.0f%%", la_var_change), `Region variance` = sprintf("%+.0f%%", reg_var_change)) |>
  kt(align = "llrrrr") |> kableExtra::collapse_rows(columns = 1, valign = "top") |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "420px")
```
